title: Sorting networks and fixed machines
sections: A comparator replaces its two input values by their minimum and maximum, with the minimum in the lower-numbered lane. A network is a fixed sequence of such comparisons, independent of the input. A sorter must finish in nondecreasing order for every input, including repeated values.

Zero–one principle: A fixed n-lane comparator network sorts every numerical input if and only if it sorts all 2ⁿ binary inputs. Thresholding each value to 0 when it is at most t and to 1 otherwise commutes with every comparator. An inverted output pair can therefore be turned into a binary inversion.

Exact small minima: Three lanes need three comparators; four lanes need five. The guide gives attaining networks. If only neighboring lanes may be compared, four lanes need six. For unrestricted networks, m swap/no-swap decisions give at most 2ᵐ histories, while sorting n distinct ranks requires at least n! different histories. The neighboring-lane bound instead counts the six inversions of 4321.

K–1: Run a fixed compare-exchange action with dot or length cards, find a failing start, and build or repair small machines. The shared launch models the compare-exchange action before a short two-bar run.
Grades 2–3: Organize complete start collections, include every binary weight, and distinguish a working construction from one proved minimal.
Grades 4–5: Connect threshold conversions to binary certification and reversible swap records to lower bounds. Small examples introduce each new notation without giving a complete sorter.

One failing input disproves a sorter claim. Many successful trials suggest a conjecture; exhaustive binary coverage plus the zero–one argument certifies all numerical inputs. A minimum also needs a lower bound. Detailed constructions and proofs follow on printed pages 3 and 9–11.
